record.tranche_reason: The study is not a double-descent reproduction, but it reports test-performance measurements across training iterations and model sizes, using its own tangent-feature analysis.
record.gate_note: Figure 6 includes test-error plots for model-size sweeps, but the text does not describe their curves or identify an interpolation threshold. Section 3.2 describes test-accuracy changes during training with label noise; it does not report a full fall-rise-fall test-error curve.
record.test_reason: The study is about tangent-kernel alignment and a proposed complexity measure. It cites Belkin et al. 2019 only for bias-variance context. Its model-size sweeps (Fig. 6) exist to compare complexity measures with the generalization gap. The text never describes a test-error peak, an interpolation threshold or a second descent. Its training-time curves (Fig. 2) show ordinary overfitting under label noise, with no second improvement reported. No result is presented as bearing on any double-descent version, so no verdicts are given.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. Tangent features align early in training with a few task-relevant directions, seen as a drop in effective rank and rising CKA with labels. The authors interpret this as feature selection and compression acting as implicit regularization. Their heuristic complexity measure correlates with the generalization gap when parameters or label corruption vary.
record.recipe_differences: The study investigates tangent-feature alignment and complexity rather than reproducing the original double-descent experiments. Its model-size sweeps and training-time performance plots are incidental to that analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports that alignment effects vary with depth and learning rate, and compares settings with different proportions of randomized labels.

fits_no_version.finding: With 50% label noise, the effective rank of the train-set tangent kernel falls during learning and rises again when test accuracy starts to drop. The authors call it a good proxy for effective capacity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The effective rank of the tangent kernel tracks the effective capacity, and the test-accuracy trajectory, of a network trained on noisy labels over training time.

fits_no_version.finding: The proposed trajectory-based complexity measure, like Neyshabur et al. 2018's, is said to reflect the shape of the generalization gap across hidden size, channel count and label corruption.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A trajectory-based tangent-kernel complexity measure correlates with the generalization gap as parameter count and label noise vary.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's relation 'tests'/T2 and its V2 limits_scope label are dropped. The study neither aims at double descent nor reports curves interpretable as testing it. Rows are kept linked to V1/V2 only as cannot_determine. Training to a fixed loss of 0.01 means all models fit the training set, so the threshold is not probed.

versions.untested_parts: The figure does not establish whether a peak occurs near the size that just fits the training set, or whether test error falls again beyond it.
The text describes a learning phase and subsequent overfitting for high label noise, but does not establish the full fall-rise-fall test-error shape.
No near-interpolation sample-size sweep is reported.
No general double-descent curve across model classes is tested.
The proposed complexity measure is compared with generalization gap, but the study does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations along size, epochs, and sample count.
Label noise is varied, but the study does not test whether it drives a double-descent peak, causes multiple peaks, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak.
The study discusses feature geometry and capacity norms but does not show that double descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve under a different parameter count.

rows.subject: VGG19
rows.operation_detail: Tracks test accuracy over SGD iterations while training with randomized labels.
rows.value: Test accuracy increases during learning and decreases when overfitting starts.
rows.note: The text describes the learning and overfitting phases, not a later second improvement in test performance; accuracy is the inverse-direction counterpart of test error.
rows.check: With 50% random labels, test accuracy rises, then falls once overfitting starts. This is the classical learn-then-memorize pattern, and no later recovery is reported up to about 1e5 iterations. The study does not frame it as epoch-wise double descent, and the plots cannot show whether a second descent would occur. It should not count as partial support.
